notable_claims: University administration deleted user files to comply with or enforce a court-ordered publication ban.
classification.summary: A report indicates that Carleton University in Canada deleted emails and files from users' home directories. The deletions targeted information related to the Homolka/Teale court case, including the text of the judge's publication ban.
classification.title: Canadian University Deleting files

notable_claims: Carleton University deleted files and emails referencing the Homolka/Teale case
Deletions were described as arbitrary and not limited to banned material
A master's student lost research files related to the case due to university deletions
classification.summary: Shawn W. Yerxa reports that Carleton University is deleting emails and directory files containing references to the Homolka/Teale case due to a Canadian court order. The author claims deletions are arbitrary and affect both personal files and academic research materials. He seeks advice on the legality of university system administrators destroying user data without warning.
classification.title: Canadian University Deleting files

notable_claims: The University of Waterloo banned specific newsgroups based on Ethics committee recommendations and legal advice due to obscene content.
classification.summary: The University of Waterloo banned several Usenet newsgroups, including alt.sex.bondage and alt.tasteless, following recommendations from its Ethics committee and legal counsel. The university cited the occasional presence of obscene material as the justification for the termination of these groups.
classification.title: directive to terminate specified newsgroups

notable_claims: The University of Waterloo administration ordered the termination of specific newsgroups from being imported to campus.
classification.summary: University of Waterloo administration issued a directive to stop importing specific Usenet newsgroups to the campus. The order was passed from the Vice-President Academic & Provost through the Associate Provost for Computing and Information Systems to technical staff.
classification.title: directive to terminate specified newsgroups

notable_claims: The University of Waterloo Ethics Committee may have treated computer-based content differently than traditional library or newspaper content.
classification.summary: A repost questioning whether the University of Waterloo Ethics Committee applied a double standard regarding obscenity. The author suggests that computer media were being treated more strictly than traditional media like libraries and student newspapers.
classification.title: obscenity - Waterloo focused on medium rather than message

notable_claims: The University of Waterloo administration considered a mechanism to block obscene newsgroups based on formal complaints.
Debate exists over whether the public display of digital content in labs constitutes a different type of offense than private reading.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the University of Waterloo's proposal to review and potentially block 'obscene' Usenet newsgroups following formal complaints. The participants debate whether censorship should focus on the content (the message) or the method of delivery (the medium), specifically addressing the public nature of computer lab displays.

notable_claims: The removal of 'Fanny Hill' from the CICA archive was a reactive response to external complaints rather than a technical decision.
University-sponsored internet archives should implement formal anti-censorship policies to protect constitutionally protected speech.
classification.summary: Jon Noring discusses the removal of a Windows Help file version of 'Fanny Hill' from the CICA archive at Indiana University following complaints from users in New Zealand. Noring argues that removing content based on complaints rather than technical specifications constitutes censorship and urges the university to adopt a formal anti-censorship policy based on ALA standards.

notable_claims: Using state-owned equipment (like a PC or office) does not necessarily obligate an individual to host all legally protected materials.
There is a fundamental tension between the use of state property and the principles of academic freedom regarding content curation.
classification.summary: Gregory R. Travis argues against the notion that an individual managing a university FTP site is constitutionally obligated to host specific content just because they use state-owned equipment. He compares the digital archive to a professor's physical office to argue that academic freedom includes the right to curate materials without being forced into 'compelled speech.' The discussion centers on whether self-censorship due to fear of institutional reprisal constitutes a legal or ethical violation of the First Amendment.
classification.title: Re: Fanny Hill Rides Again!

identity.subject: Re: Fanny Hill Rides Again! (was Re: Censor on Internet..Pt-1)

notable_claims: The University is at risk of prosecution if it knowingly distributes obscene material.
The Supreme Court of Canada upheld obscenity provisions as a justifiable restriction on freedom of expression.
classification.summary: James Downey, President of the University of Waterloo, announced a process for restricting Internet newsgroups containing material deemed obscene under the Canadian Criminal Code. The policy establishes an Ethics Committee to review complaints and recommend removals to the Vice-President Academic & Provost. This action was framed as a necessary legal protection for the university despite concerns regarding academic free speech.
classification.title: Newsgroups on the Internet

notable_claims: Files were only removed from public areas, not individual accounts on the FreeNet machine.
classification.summary: A repost clarifies a distinction between university-owned machines and FreeNet machines regarding account ownership. The Chairman of the National Capital FreeNet asserts that while they reserve the right to delete files, they have only removed files from public areas rather than individual accounts.
classification.title: Canadian University Deleting files

notable_claims: The National Capital FreeNet user agreement allows the board to remove material it deems unlawful, obscene, or objectionable.
Materials from a New York Times article were removed due to a publication ban and copyright violation.
classification.summary: Shawn W. Yerxa alleged that Carleton University was arbitrarily deleting files and emails related to the Homolka/Teale court case publication ban. Dave Sutherland clarified that the hardware was owned by the National Capital FreeNet (NCF), not the university, and that NCF removed specific materials to comply with a legal publication ban and copyright claims.
classification.title: Re: Canadian University Deleting files
